nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-01.title: Total weight
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-01.body:
The girls weigh $12\cdot120=1440$ in total and the boys $18\cdot150=2700$. The average of all $30$ students is $\frac{1440+2700}{30}=\frac{4140}{30}=138$.

**Answer: 138**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-01.title: Weighted average
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-01.body:
The boys make up $\frac{18}{30}=\frac35$ of the class, so the average is $120+\frac35(150-120)=120+18=138$.

**Answer: 138**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-02.title: Pythagorean theorem
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-02.body:
Let $R$ and $r$ be the radii. The radius of the small circle to the point of tangency is perpendicular to the chord and bisects it, so $5^2+r^2=R^2$. The area between the circles is $\pi(R^2-r^2)=25\pi$.

**Answer: $25\pi$**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-03.title: Symmetry
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-03.body:
There are $6!=720$ line-ups. Swapping Arthur and Jeffrey pairs each line-up where Arthur is ahead with one where Jeffrey is ahead, so exactly half, $360$, have Arthur in front of Jeffrey.

If "in front of" is read as *immediately* in front, glue Arthur–Jeffrey into one block: $5!=120$ line-ups. The official correction accepts both $360$ and $120$.

**Answer: 360**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-08.title: Expand in base b
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-08.body:
$(3b^2+2b)+(4b^2+3b)=b^3+3b^2$, so $b^3-4b^2-5b=0$, i.e. $b(b-5)(b+1)=0$. The base must exceed the digit $4$, so $b=5$.

**Answer: 5**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-08.title: Add column by column
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-08.body:
Units: $0+0=0$. $b$'s column: $2+3=5$, which must give digit $0$ with carry $1$, so $b=5$. Check: $b^2$ column $3+4+1=8=1\cdot5+3$, digit $3$ carry $1$, matching $1300_5$.

**Answer: 5**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-09.title: Triangular numbers
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-09.body:
The sums $\frac{N(N+1)}{2}$ for $N=2,3,\dots$ are $3,6,10,15,21,28,36,\dots$. The first perfect square is $36=6^2$, at $N=8$.

**Answer: 8**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-10.title: Add rates
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-10.body:
If Mary takes $m$ hours, the rates are $\frac1m$, $\frac1{2m}$, $\frac1{3m}$ jobs per hour, totaling $\frac{6+3+2}{6m}=\frac{11}{6m}$. Working together takes $2$ hours: $\frac{11}{6m}=\frac12$, so $m=\frac{11}3$ hours.

**Answer: $\frac{11}{3}$ hours**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-10.title: Mary-equivalents
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-10.body:
In the time Mary does $1$ job, Cindy does $\frac12$ and David $\frac13$, so together they work like $\frac{11}{6}$ Marys. A job taking the team $2$ hours takes Mary alone $2\cdot\frac{11}{6}=\frac{11}{3}$ hours.

**Answer: $\frac{11}{3}$ hours**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-11.title: Slopes
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-11.body:
The slopes are $-\frac34$ and $-\frac5a$. Perpendicular lines have slopes with product $-1$: $\frac{15}{4a}=-1$, so $a=-\frac{15}4$.

**Answer: $-\frac{15}{4}$**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-11.title: Normal vectors
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-11.body:
The normal vectors $(3,4)$ and $(5,a)$ must be perpendicular: $15+4a=0$, $a=-\frac{15}{4}$.

**Answer: $-\frac{15}{4}$**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-12.title: Count odd sums
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-12.body:
There are $8$ odd and $7$ even balls. The sum is odd when $1$ or $3$ of the balls are odd: $\binom81\binom72+\binom83=168+56=224$ of the $\binom{15}3=455$ possible sets. The probability is $\frac{224}{455}=\frac{32}{65}$.

**Answer: $\frac{224}{455}=\frac{32}{65}$**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-14.title: Project the sides
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-14.body:
Let the rectangle have sides $PQ=RS=L$ and $QR=SP=W$, with $P$ on the bottom side and $PQ$ making angle $\theta$ with it. Then $SP\perp PQ$ makes angle $90^\circ-\theta$ with the bottom side. Projecting onto the bottom and right sides of the square:
$$L\cos\theta+W\sin\theta=10,\qquad L\sin\theta+W\cos\theta=10.$$
Subtracting: $(L-W)(\cos\theta-\sin\theta)=0$. The rectangle is not a square, so $L\ne W$ and $\theta=45^\circ$. Adding: $(L+W)(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)=20$, so $(L+W)\sqrt2=20$ and $L+W=10\sqrt2$. The perimeter is $2(L+W)=20\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $20\sqrt2$**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-14.title: Sides parallel to the diagonals
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-14.body:
Such a rectangle has sides parallel to the square's diagonals, so each corner of the square cuts off an isosceles right triangle. A side of the rectangle cutting off legs $t$ has length $t\sqrt2$; along each side of the square the two legs add to $10$. So two adjacent sides of the rectangle have total length $10\sqrt2$, and the perimeter is $20\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $20\sqrt2$**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-15.title: Middle term
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-15.body:
The middle term is the average of its neighbours: $2(x+2)=(x-1)+(3x+7)$, so $2x+4=4x+6$ and $x=-1$. (Terms: $-2,1,4$.)

**Answer: $-1$**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-16.title: Prime exponents
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-16.body:
$2250=2\cdot3^2\cdot5^3$. For a fourth power every exponent must be a multiple of $4$, so the smallest $x$ is $2^3\cdot3^2\cdot5=360$, giving $2250\cdot360=2^4 3^4 5^4=30^4$.

**Answer: 360**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-17.title: Tangent addition
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-17.body:
$\tan(\arctan\frac12+\arctan\frac13)=\frac{\frac12+\frac13}{1-\frac16}=\frac{5/6}{5/6}=1$. Both angles are between $0^\circ$ and $45^\circ$, so the sum is $45^\circ$.

**Answer: $45^\circ$**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-18.title: Right triangle
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-18.body:
Since $3^2+4^2=5^2$, angle $C$ is right and $AB$ is the hypotenuse. The median to the hypotenuse is half of it, so $AM=\frac52$. In a right triangle $AC^2=AD\cdot AB$, so $AD=\frac95$. Then $DM=AM-AD=\frac52-\frac95=\frac7{10}$.

**Answer: $\frac{7}{10}$**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-18.title: Coordinates
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-18.body:
Put $C=(0,0)$, $A=(3,0)$, $B=(0,4)$. Then $M=\left(\frac32,2\right)$ and the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $4x+3y=12$ is $D=\left(\frac{48}{25},\frac{36}{25}\right)$. So $DM=\sqrt{\left(\frac{48}{25}-\frac{75}{50}\right)^2+\left(\frac{36}{25}-2\right)^2}=\sqrt{\left(\frac{21}{50}\right)^2+\left(\frac{28}{50}\right)^2}=\frac{35}{50}=\frac7{10}$.

**Answer: $\frac{7}{10}$**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-20.title: Binomial
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-20.body:
Each roll succeeds with probability $\frac13$. "At least half" of $5$ rolls means at least $3$:
$$\binom53\frac{2^2}{3^5}+\binom54\frac{2}{3^5}+\binom55\frac1{3^5}=\frac{40+10+1}{243}=\frac{51}{243}=\frac{17}{81}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{17}{81}$**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-21.title: Pythagorean theorem
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-21.body:
With width $w$ and length $6w$: $w^2+36w^2=25$, so $w^2=\frac{25}{37}$. The area is $6w^2=\frac{150}{37}$.

**Answer: $\frac{150}{37}$**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-23.title: Exterior angles
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-23.body:
Each exterior angle is $180^\circ-174^\circ=6^\circ$, and the exterior angles total $360^\circ$, so there are $\frac{360}{6}=60$ sides.

**Answer: 60**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-24.title: Base times height
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-24.body:
The base is equilateral with side $2$, area $\sqrt3$. The apex lies above the centroid, which is $\frac23\cdot\sqrt3=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$ from each base vertex, so the height is $\sqrt{4-\frac43}=\sqrt{\frac83}$. The volume is $\frac13\cdot\sqrt3\cdot\sqrt{\frac83}=\frac{\sqrt8}{3}=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{3}\sqrt8=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-24.title: Inside a cube
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-24.body:
A regular tetrahedron of edge $2$ is formed by four alternate vertices of a cube of edge $\sqrt2$. Removing the four corner pyramids, each of volume $\frac16(\sqrt2)^3$, leaves $(\sqrt2)^3\left(1-\frac46\right)=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-25.title: Set up the digits
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-25.body:
$10a+b=3(a+b)$ gives $7a=2b$. With digits $a\ge1$, $b\le9$: $a=2$, $b=7$. The number is $27$ ($3\cdot9=27$).

**Answer: 27**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-26.title: Binomial pattern
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-26.body:
The left side is $(x+1)^4$. So $(x+1)^4=16$, giving $(x+1)^2=4$ (since $(x+1)^2=-4$ has no real solutions), so $x+1=\pm2$: $x=1$ or $x=-3$.

**Answer: $1$ and $-3$**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-27.title: Drop heights
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-27.body:
The bases are $7$ and $15$ and the legs are $5$. Dropping perpendiculars from the ends of the short base cuts off $\frac{15-7}2=4$ on each side, so the height is $\sqrt{25-16}=3$. A diagonal spans horizontally $15-4=11$ and vertically $3$: its length is $\sqrt{121+9}=\sqrt{130}$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{130}$**

nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-27.title: Ptolemy
nyciml-1993-94-spring-seniorb-27.body:
An isosceles trapezoid is cyclic, so Ptolemy's theorem gives $d^2=7\cdot15+5\cdot5=130$ and $d=\sqrt{130}$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{130}$**
